content: The susceptibility of Leishmania donovani in South-East Asia to low-dose liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) presents a unique opportunity for primary prophylaxis in asymptomatic patients co-infected with Leishmania and HIV. This approach could potentially reduce the progression to symptomatic visceral leishmaniasis (VL) and warrants further investigation. Recent evidence suggests that maintaining specific immunity to leishmaniasis and ensuring an undetectable HIV viral load are critical factors in keeping patients asymptomatic for VL. Basic research is needed to better understand the immunological interactions between the two infections and the immune-modulatory effects of drugs. This could ultimately improve the management of co-infection. Given the current low certainty of available evidence, further clinical trials on the use of combination therapy in VL-HIV co-infection are essential. Well-designed studies are urgently required to strengthen the evidence base for treatment and improve patient outcomes, particularly in field conditions in East Africa and South-East Asia. The development of more user-friendly and oral medications must continue, as ease of use remains a priority. None of the current antileishmanial drugs are free from significant toxicity, making the safety of treatment regimens a critical area of research. Traditional pharmacovigilance approaches provide limited information, and cohort event monitoring may offer more reliable safety data. There is no available data on the safety of miltefosine therapy beyond 28 days. Studies on the safety of long-term miltefosine treatment are necessary, as VL patients may require extended therapy or multiple cycles in cases of relapse. Additional interventions to improve the efficacy of antileishmanial treatment are needed to reduce relapses, prevent resistance, and minimize toxicity. Research should explore early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), the use of combined antileishmanial therapies in various scenarios, and immune-based co-therapies. To date, there is no clear evidence on the interaction between antiretroviral drugs and antileishmanial medications. Further evidence is required to establish criteria for the use of drugs in secondary prophylaxis. Secondary prophylaxis with a drug different from the one used to treat the primary VL episode is generally recommended to minimize resistance risk, with clear starting and stopping criteria. This is particularly important in South-East Asia, where evidence for secondary prophylaxis is limited. Simpler therapeutic and prophylactic regimens for VL-HIV co-infected patients are also needed. Social determinants of VL in HIV patients remain poorly explored, and more studies are required. Given the focal distribution of VL-HIV co-infection and the difficulty in accessing hard-to-reach populations, conducting research is inherently challenging. Operational and implementation research on systematic screening models for VL among HIV patients and vice versa will facilitate both research and program implementation. Scientific research to better understand the impact of VL-HIV co-infection, improve program efficiency, and reduce mortality would further inform policymakers. Research to understand the perspectives of affected communities is also important to reduce delays in accessing healthcare services. The WHO guidelines will be made accessible on their website, translated into official United Nations languages relevant to VL and HIV, and distributed through national leishmaniasis control programs to health staff managing cases. WHO regional offices will ensure dissemination to country offices, ministries of health, and key international and national organizations. Additional tools will be developed to support country implementation. The incorporation of VL into national treatment protocols and field implementation will be monitored through existing support activities and the annual WHO coordination meeting on VL. The use of these guidelines will be evaluated to determine the extent of their adoption into national policies and programs. Results will be published annually in WHO reports, leishmaniasis surveillance updates, and country profiles in co-endemic regions. New evidence and evaluation results will inform future updates.
